q.q: What forms the buses that link the components on a motherboard?
o: Cables plugged into the ports
Registers inside the processor
Pulses sent out by the clock
Copper tracks printed on the board
q.why: The motherboard is a printed circuit board; its copper tracks form the buses.

q.q: A pupil lists the computer's SSD as part of main memory. Why is this wrong?
o: Main memory is RAM and ROM, which the processor addresses directly
Main memory is only the cache built into the processor chip
An SSD is volatile, so it cannot be counted as memory
Main memory is the registers, which hold the data in use
q.why: An SSD or hard disk is secondary storage, reached through an I/O controller.

q.q: Which two of the internal components are part of the processor itself?
o: The main memory and the ports
The I/O controllers and the buses
The registers and the clock
The RAM and the ROM chips
q.why: Registers and the clock are part of the processor; memory, controllers and ports are separate components linked by the system bus.

q.q: What must happen before the processor can run an app that is stored on the SSD?
o: The OS copies its instructions from secondary storage into RAM
The processor copies the app into its registers in one step
The I/O controller converts the app into hexadecimal
The clock loads the app into ROM so it is not lost
q.why: The processor can only fetch instructions directly from main memory.

q.q: Which is NOT a task of the control unit?
o: Managing the fetch–decode–execute cycle
Carrying out arithmetic and comparisons
Sending control signals to coordinate hardware
Controlling the movement of data in and out
q.why: The CU directs; the ALU calculates and compares.

q.q: A program contains if (score >= 50). Which part of the processor carries out the comparison?
o: The control unit
The arithmetic logic unit
The program counter
The memory data register
q.why: Comparisons are logical operations done by the ALU; the CU uses the result to decide which instruction comes next.

q.q: After the ALU carries out an operation, where is the result usually placed?
o: The accumulator
The program counter
The memory address register
The current instruction register
q.why: The ALU writes its result back to a register, usually the accumulator.

q.q: A pupil writes total = total + price; in C#. How are the processor's registers handled for this line?
o: The C# programmer names the registers in the source code
The compiler produces instructions that load and use the registers
The registers are not used, as C# works directly on RAM
The control unit performs the addition inside the clock
q.why: Only machine code and assembly handle registers directly; the compiler generates that code.

q.q: What does the memory address register hold?
o: The data or instruction just read from memory
The address of the location about to be read or written
The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The instruction currently being decoded
q.why: The MAR always holds an address, which it places on the address bus.

q.q: Which register acts as a two-way buffer between the processor and memory and is also called the memory buffer register?
o: Memory address register (MAR)
Current instruction register (CIR)
Memory data register (MDR)
Accumulator (ACC)
q.why: The MDR holds data or an instruction just read from memory, or data waiting to be written.

q.q: Which register's contents are split by the control unit into opcode and operand?
o: Current instruction register (CIR)
Memory data register (MDR)
Program counter (PC)
Memory address register (MAR)
q.why: The CIR holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

q.q: Each instruction occupies one address. While the instruction at address 40 is being executed, what does the program counter normally hold?
q.why: The PC is incremented during the fetch, so it already points to the following instruction.

q.q: Why is the address bus unidirectional?
o: Memory sends addresses back to the processor
Addresses are too large to travel both ways
Only the processor chooses which location to use
It shares its lines with the control bus
q.why: Addresses travel only from the CPU to memory or I/O; memory never sends an address back.

q.q: Which of these does NOT travel on the control bus?
o: A memory write signal
A clock signal
The address of the location to be read
An interrupt request
q.why: Addresses use the address bus; the control bus carries read, write, clock and interrupt signals.

q.q: A printer signals the processor that it has finished a job. Which bus carries the signal, and in which direction?
o: The control bus, into the processor
The address bus, into the processor
The data bus, out from the processor
The control bus, out from the processor
q.why: The control bus is two-way overall: some signals, such as interrupts, come in to the CPU.

q.q: What does the width of a bus describe?
o: The length of the tracks between the components
The number of parallel lines, so the bits carried at once
The number of devices connected to the bus
The clock speed at which the bus transfers data
q.why: Each line carries one bit, so the number of lines sets how many bits travel together.

q.q: A computer has a 16-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. What is its maximum addressable memory?
o: 512 KB
128 KB
64 KB
16 KB
q.why: 2¹⁶ × 8 bits = 2¹⁹ bits = 2¹⁶ bytes = 64 KB. 512 KB forgets to divide by 8.

q.q: A computer has a 24-bit address bus and a 16-bit data bus. What is its maximum addressable memory?
o: 32 MB
256 MB
16 MB
48 MB
q.why: 2²⁴ × 2⁴ bits = 2²⁸ bits = 2²⁵ bytes = 32 MB. 256 MB forgets to divide by 8.

q.q: A computer has a 32-bit data bus and a maximum addressable memory of 4 MB. How wide is its address bus?
o: 22 bits
25 bits
17 bits
20 bits
q.why: 4 MB = 2²² bytes = 2²⁵ bits; 2²⁵ ÷ 2⁵ = 2²⁰ locations, so 20 address lines.

q.q: What is the minimum address bus width needed to address 3000 memory locations?
o: 11 bits
13 bits
10 bits
12 bits
q.why: 2¹¹ = 2048 is too few; 2¹² = 4096 is enough.

q.q: Which I/O controller task stops a fast processor being held up by a slow printer?
o: Buffering
Voltage conversion
Protocol conversion
Data format conversion
q.why: The controller stores data temporarily so the processor can carry on with other work.

q.q: A sensor signals at a voltage that would damage the computer. Which I/O controller task deals with this?
o: Buffering
Protocol conversion
Voltage conversion
Data format conversion
q.why: The controller converts the device's signal to a level safe for the computer.

q.q: A device sends 16-bit values but the computer expects 32-bit values. Which I/O controller task deals with this?
o: Data format conversion
Protocol conversion
Voltage conversion
Buffering
q.why: Data format conversion changes data into the form the computer expects.

q.q: What is the main advantage of the USB standard for ports?
o: Each device type has its own dedicated socket
It removes the need for an I/O controller
It connects devices directly to the processor
One standard connector carries both data and power
q.why: USB defines cables, connectors and protocols for data and power through one connector.

q.q: Why does the stored-program concept make a computer general purpose?
o: Instructions and data are kept in separate memories so both can be fetched
Programs are fixed in ROM so they cannot be changed by accident
To change what it does you load different instructions rather than rewiring it
Every program is executed in parallel on its own processor
q.why: Instructions are held in memory as binary like data, so a new program is simply loaded.

q.q: What causes the Von Neumann bottleneck?
o: Instructions and data share one memory and one bus
The processor has too few registers
Secondary storage is used to keep programs
The clock speed is limited by heat
q.why: Instructions and data cannot be fetched at the same time, so the fast processor waits for memory.

q.q: Which is a feature of the Von Neumann architecture?
o: Instructions and data are kept in separate memories
Instructions and data travel on separate buses
Instruction memory cannot be used to hold data
A single processor executes instructions in sequence
q.why: Von Neumann uses one processor, one shared memory and one shared bus; the others describe Harvard.

q.q: Which design change helps reduce the Von Neumann bottleneck?
o: Storing programs on secondary storage rather than in memory
Removing the control bus so that only data is transferred
Combining the address bus and data bus into a single bus
Adding cache memory and splitting it into instruction and data caches
q.why: Cache, wider buses and separate instruction and data caches all reduce waiting for memory.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the fetch stage?
o: PC ← [PC] + 1; MAR ← [PC]; CIR ← [Memory[MAR]]; MDR ← [CIR]
MAR ← [PC]; PC ← [PC] + 1; MDR ← [Memory[MAR]]; CIR ← [MDR]
MDR ← [PC]; MAR ← [MDR]; PC ← [PC] + 1; CIR ← [MAR]
MAR ← [PC]; CIR ← [Memory[MAR]]; MDR ← [CIR]; PC ← [PC] + 1
q.why: The PC is copied to the MAR, the PC incremented, the instruction read into the MDR and copied to the CIR.

q.q: In the instruction ADD 21, which part is the operand?
o: ADD, the operation to be performed
21, the address where the value is held
The accumulator, where the result goes
The program counter, which points to it
q.why: The opcode is the operation (ADD); the operand is the value or address it acts on.

q.q: Which register transfers carry out the execute stage of ADD 21?
o: PC ← 21; CIR ← [Memory[21]]; ACC ← [ACC] + [CIR]
MDR ← 21; MAR ← [Memory[21]]; ACC ← [ACC] + [MAR]
MAR ← 21; MDR ← [Memory[21]]; ACC ← [ACC] + [MDR]
MAR ← [PC]; MDR ← [Memory[MAR]]; ACC ← [MDR]
q.why: The address goes to the MAR, the value is read into the MDR, and the ALU adds it to the accumulator.

q.q: Why will machine code written for one processor family not run on another?
o: Each family uses a different clock speed
Machine code is stored in hexadecimal
Each family recognises its own instruction set
Each family has a different number of cores
q.why: The opcodes one family decodes mean nothing, or something else, to another.

q.q: With three single-unit stages, how many time units do 10 instructions take with pipelining?
q.why: n + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12. 30 is the time without pipelining.

q.q: With three single-unit stages, how many time units does pipelining save for 20 instructions?
Which statement about pipelining is correct?
o: Each instruction now takes one unit from fetch to execute
It works by raising the clock speed of the processor
It is most effective when a program has many jumps
Each instruction still takes three units from fetch to execute
q.why: Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of an individual instruction.

q.q: What happens to the pipeline when a jump instruction is executed?
o: It is paused until the clock speed increases
The jump is executed in parallel on another core
The next instruction is skipped but the rest stay
It is flushed and refilled from the new address
q.why: The instructions already fetched and decoded behind the jump may be wrong, so they are discarded.

q.q: How long does one clock cycle last on a 3.2 GHz processor?
o: 3.2 ns

q.q: Which statement about 32-bit and 64-bit software is correct?
o: A 32-bit processor runs 64-bit software, but not the reverse
Neither processor can run the other type of software
Both run either type equally well with no limitations
A 64-bit processor runs 32-bit software, but not the reverse
q.why: 64-bit programs cannot run on a 32-bit processor; a 64-bit processor can run 32-bit software.

q.q: When is comparing clock speeds a fair way to compare two processors?
o: When both processors are of a similar design
When both processors have different numbers of cores
When one is RISC and the other is CISC
When both processors have the same cache size
q.why: Different designs do different amounts of work per cycle, so clock speed only compares fairly between similar designs.

q.q: What is a processor's word size?
o: The number of cores on the chip
The number of bits it treats as one unit
The number of clock cycles per second
The amount of cache memory it has
q.why: Word size matches the width of the general registers, e.g. 64 bits.

q.q: What is the effect of widening the address bus?
o: Each transfer moves more bits at once
The clock can run at a higher speed
Instructions are decoded more quickly
More memory can be fitted and addressed
q.why: A wider address bus identifies more locations; it does not make a single transfer faster.

q.q: How many transfers does a 32-bit data bus need to move 64 bytes?
q.why: A 32-bit bus moves 4 bytes per transfer: 64 ÷ 4 = 16. A 64-bit bus would need 8.

q.q: Why does adding more and more cache eventually bring little extra benefit?
o: Once the repeatedly used items fit, extra cache adds little
Cache becomes slower than RAM once it grows too large
The processor can only use the first megabyte of cache
Larger caches reduce the clock speed of the processor
q.why: There are diminishing returns, and cache is expensive.

q.q: A PC with too little RAM is swapping constantly to a slow hard disk. Why would fitting a faster processor help very little?
o: The processor would still wait for pages to be swapped
A faster processor would need a wider address bus
Faster processors cannot use virtual memory
A faster processor would use less cache
q.why: Upgrading one part just moves the bottleneck; the system is limited by swapping.

q.q: Why can a quad-core 2.4 GHz processor out-perform a single-core 3.5 GHz processor?
o: A lower clock speed always means more work per cycle
Quad-core chips do not need a clock signal at all
On multi-threaded work four cores run threads at once
Clock speed is measured differently on multi-core chips
q.why: Clock speed alone ignores cores, cache, pipelining and work done per cycle.

q.q: What does MIPS stand for?
o: Memory instructions per second
Multiple instruction processing speed
Megabits of input per second
Millions of instructions per second
q.why: MIPS measures how quickly general instructions are executed.

q.q: A company is choosing a file server. Why would comparing MIPS figures alone be misleading?
o: MIPS only measures floating-point arithmetic
MIPS is only used to rate graphics cards
MIPS says nothing about disk or network speed
MIPS is measured in bytes, not instructions
q.why: MIPS and FLOPS describe the processor only; a file server depends heavily on storage and network speed.

q.q: Which measure is most relevant when comparing processors for 3D graphics and scientific modelling?
o: MIPS
Clock speed
FLOPS
Word size
q.why: FLOPS measures arithmetic on real numbers; GPUs are rated in teraFLOPS.

q.q: A laptop specification lists '16 GB RAM'. How many bytes is this?
o: 16 × 10⁹ bytes
16 × 2²⁰ bytes
16 × 2³⁰ bytes
16 × 2³⁰ bits
q.why: Memory sizes use binary multiples: 1 GB = 2³⁰ bytes.

q.q: A media studies class edits video using multi-threaded software. Laptop A is 3.4 GHz dual-core; laptop B is 3.0 GHz quad-core, same design. Which is the better choice?
o: A, because a higher clock speed always wins
B, because its four cores can render in parallel
A, because video editing uses only one core
B, because quad-core chips have a faster clock
q.why: Multi-threaded rendering can use all four cores, outweighing the small clock difference.

q.q: What does '512 GB SSD' in a specification mean for performance?
o: Main memory that holds the programs currently in use
Flash storage that loads the OS and files quickly, with no moving parts
Cache memory that reduces slow trips to RAM
A hard disk that spins its platters faster
q.why: An SSD is flash secondary storage; RAM and cache are different parts of the specification.

q.q: A specification lists '12 MB cache'. Which cache does this figure usually describe?
o: The L1 cache of each core
The shared L3 cache
The L2 cache of one core
The disk's buffer memory
q.why: The headline cache figure is usually the shared L3, the largest cache level.

q.q: Which is the best way to state a difference between RAM and ROM?
o: RAM is volatile whereas ROM is non-volatile
RAM is non-volatile whereas ROM is volatile
RAM is secondary storage whereas ROM is main memory
RAM holds start-up firmware whereas ROM holds open files
q.why: Comparison answers need an explicit contrast; RAM loses its contents without power, ROM keeps them.

q.q: In a PC, what does ROM store?
o: The whole operating system while it is running
The documents the user is currently editing
Pages swapped out of RAM when it is full
The start-up firmware that loads the operating system
q.why: ROM's firmware tests the hardware and loads the OS from secondary storage into RAM.

q.q: Where is the program in a dishwasher's controller most likely to be stored?
o: RAM, as the program is in use
Cache, as the program runs often
ROM, as the program never changes
Virtual memory on a hard disk
q.why: Fixed embedded programs are kept in non-volatile ROM (or flash).

q.q: Why do many modern devices hold their start-up firmware in flash memory rather than traditional ROM?
o: So that the firmware can be updated
So that the firmware is lost at power-off
So that the processor can run faster
So that more RAM slots are available
q.why: Flash is non-volatile but rewritable, allowing firmware updates.

q.q: What is a cache hit?
o: The item the processor needs is already in cache
The item is fetched from RAM and copied into cache
The cache is full and an item must be removed
The processor writes a result back to RAM
q.why: On a hit the item arrives almost immediately; a miss means fetching it from RAM.

q.q: Which level of cache is usually shared by all the cores?
o: L1
L2
The register file
L3
q.why: L1 is per core and fastest, L2 usually per core, L3 the largest and shared.

q.q: Which list orders storage from fastest to slowest?
o: Cache, registers, RAM, secondary storage
Registers, RAM, cache, secondary storage
RAM, cache, registers, secondary storage
Registers, cache, RAM, secondary storage
q.why: In the memory hierarchy, the closer to the processor, the faster, smaller and more expensive per byte.

q.q: Why does cache work especially well for the instructions inside a loop?
o: The same instructions are used over and over
Loop instructions are kept in ROM
Loops never need data from memory
The cache is non-volatile
q.why: Cache stores frequently used instructions and data, so repeated loop instructions are served quickly.

q.q: In virtual memory, what is a page?
o: A single register in the processor
One sector on a hard disk track
A program waiting in the queue
A fixed-size block of memory
q.why: Memory is managed in fixed-size blocks called pages, which are swapped between RAM and disk.

q.q: Which sequence correctly describes virtual memory in use?
o: RAM full; inactive pages copied to disk; copied back when needed
Cache full; pages copied to RAM; copied back to cache when needed
Disk full; files copied to RAM; copied back at shut-down
RAM full; the newest program is closed to free space
q.why: Inactive pages go to the page file and return to RAM when needed, perhaps pushing another page out.

q.q: A PC's hard disk is replaced by an SSD. What is the effect on virtual memory?
o: Virtual memory becomes as fast as RAM
Virtual memory is no longer needed at all
Swapping becomes slower than before
Swapping is less slow, but still much slower than RAM
q.why: An SSD makes swapping less painful but is still far slower than RAM.

q.q: Which is an advantage of virtual memory?
o: More programs can be open than physical RAM allows
It is faster than adding more physical RAM
It removes the risk of disk thrashing
It stops the processor waiting for data
q.why: It extends capacity using cheap disk space, at the cost of speed.

q.q: Which of these is a factor in choosing a storage device, rather than a benefit of secondary storage?
o: Durability
Security through backups
Capacity beyond that of RAM
Permanence after switch-off
q.why: Choice factors are speed, capacity, durability, portability, reliability and cost.

q.q: Why do organisations keep copies of data on secondary storage off-site?
o: To make the data faster to access each day
Because off-site storage is always volatile
To protect it from fire or theft at the main site
To reduce the amount of RAM that is needed
q.why: Off-site backups provide security if the main site is damaged.

q.q: Why is internal storage usually faster than external storage?
o: It always uses flash memory rather than disks
It is volatile, so data is read more quickly
It has a larger capacity than external devices
It connects directly to the motherboard's internal interface
q.why: External devices go through a port such as USB or over a network.

q.q: A wildlife photographer works outdoors and travels between countries. Which two factors matter most in her choice of storage?
o: Capacity and serial access
Portability and durability
Cost and volatility
Reliability and read-only access
q.why: Her storage must be easy to carry and survive knocks and the weather.

q.q: How is the surface of a hard disk platter organised?
o: Into a single spiral track read by a laser
Into concentric tracks, each divided into sectors
Into rows of semiconductor cells
Into a long strip read from start to end
q.why: Each surface has concentric tracks, each divided into sectors.

q.q: Why does a hard disk provide direct access?
o: The head can move straight to any track
It must wind through earlier data first
It has no moving parts to slow it down
Each file is stored in a separate chip
q.why: The actuator arm moves the head straight to the required track; tape must wind through in order.

q.q: Approximately how much data does a single-layer Blu-ray disc hold?
o: 4.7 GB
700 MB
25 GB
128 GB
q.why: Blu-ray holds 25 GB per layer; 4.7 GB is a DVD and up to 128 GB needs four layers.

q.q: A computer has only a CD-ROM drive. Why can it not back up files to a blank CD-R?
o: CD-R discs can only be written at manufacture
A CD-ROM drive can read discs but cannot write
CD-R discs hold too little for any backup
A CD-ROM drive can only read DVDs
q.why: The drive, not the disc, is the problem: a CD-ROM drive cannot write.

q.q: How do SSDs make up for each flash cell being rewritable only a limited number of times?
o: They store each bit magnetically as well
They write data to RAM instead
They spread writes across the cells
They use a laser to refresh cells
q.why: The drive spreads writes across its cells so that no cells wear out early.

q.q: Why does an SSD give a laptop longer battery life than a hard disk?
o: It holds more data in the same space
It uses less power, as no motors spin platters
It is cheaper per gigabyte
It stores data as magnetised regions
q.why: A hard disk's motors draw power; flash has no moving parts.

q.q: Which answer would earn the mark for explaining why an SSD has faster access than a hard disk?
o: It is faster, because SSDs are a newer and better technology
It has no moving parts, so there is no head to move or platter to spin
It is faster, because it costs more per gigabyte to buy
It has faster access, because it is volatile like RAM
q.why: The mark comes from the reason: no seek time or rotational delay.

q.q: A drone records video to a removable card. Which storage is it most likely to use?
o: A small magnetic hard disk
A microSD flash memory card
A rewritable DVD
A magnetic tape cartridge
q.why: Memory cards are small, light, robust and portable, ideal for drones and cameras.

q.q: A firm's full backup is restored only in an emergency. Why is magnetic tape suitable?
o: Tape gives the fastest direct access to individual files
Tape is the most portable medium for daily use
Serial access does not matter for rare restores, and tape is cheap for large capacity
Tape can only be written once, so it cannot be changed
q.why: Serial access is a poor fit for files used often, but fine for an occasional restore.

q.q: A software company distributes a user guide that must not be altered. Which medium suits this?
o: Rewritable USB flash drive
Internal SSD in the customer's PC
Write-once optical disc such as a CD-R
Magnetic tape cartridge
q.why: A write-once disc protects a distributed file from change and is cheap to post.

q.q: A vet practice's main PC must open patient records quickly all day. Which medium is best for the working files?
o: Magnetic tape, as it has very low cost per GB
An internal SSD, as it has the fastest access
A DVD-R, as it cannot be altered
A CD-RW, as it is easy to post
q.why: Speed is the main need for working files, so SSD is the best match.

q.q: Which is a drawback of cloud storage for backups?
o: It depends on an internet connection and trust in the provider
It offers no off-site protection against fire
It cannot be shared with other users
It is limited to serial access only
q.why: Cloud adds off-site protection and sharing but needs a connection and trust.

q.q: A job takes 100 s; 80 s of it can be split across cores and the rest is sequential. Ideally, how long does it take on 4 cores?
q.why: 20 s sequential + 80 ÷ 4 = 20 s parallel = 40 s. 25 s wrongly assumes the whole job can be split.

q.q: Which limitation of parallel processing arises from dividing the work and combining the results?
o: The sequential part of the task
The Von Neumann bottleneck
Limited write cycles of the cores
Overheads of coordinating the cores
q.why: Splitting, coordinating and recombining all take time, reducing the speed-up.

q.q: In a multi-core processor, which part is usually shared by the cores?
o: The control unit
The ALU
The L1 cache
The L3 cache
q.why: Each core has its own CU, ALU, registers and L1 cache, and they usually share a larger L3.

q.q: Which is a benefit of adding cores rather than raising the clock speed?
o: More work per second with less extra heat
Sequential tasks run several times faster
Software no longer needs to use threads
Cores no longer compete for shared memory
q.why: Parallel cores do more work without the heat and power of a much faster clock.

q.q: What allows a Harvard-architecture processor to fetch an instruction and its data at the same time?
o: A single shared bus that is twice as wide
A larger L3 cache shared by all cores
Storing instructions and data in the same RAM
Separate memories and buses for instructions and data
q.why: With separate paths, both fetches can happen together, avoiding the Von Neumann bottleneck.

q.q: Which is an advantage of Harvard architecture in a microcontroller?
o: Spare instruction memory can be used to hold extra data
It is simpler and cheaper to build than Von Neumann
Any location can hold either code or data
Program and data memories can be of different types and word lengths
q.why: For example, the program can sit in flash and the data in a small RAM. The other options describe Von Neumann.

q.q: How does a modern PC processor gain some of the Harvard architecture's speed?
o: Its L1 cache is split into separate instruction and data caches
Its main RAM is split into instruction and data chips
It has no shared system bus to main memory
It stores all programs in ROM rather than RAM
q.why: A PC is Von Neumann at main memory but each core's split L1 cache lets it fetch both at once.

q.q: Which is an acceptable example of a computer using the Harvard architecture?
o: A desktop PC
A digital signal processor
A laptop running Windows
A web server

q.q: In a RISC processor, which instructions access memory?
o: Every arithmetic instruction
Only the complex instructions
Only LOAD and STORE
Only jump instructions

q.q: A CISC processor multiplies two values with MULT 22, 20, 21, while a RISC processor needs LOAD, LOAD, MUL and STORE. What does this show?
o: CISC programs are shorter, but each instruction does more work
RISC programs are shorter, as each instruction does more
CISC instructions are all executed in a single cycle
RISC cannot multiply values held in memory

q.q: Why do x86 (CISC) processors remain common in desktop PCs?
o: CISC processors use less power than RISC processors
CISC instructions are easier to pipeline than RISC ones
x86 processors have the fewest instructions available
Decades of Windows software expect the x86 instruction set

RISC processors now use variable-length instructions
CISC processors no longer support pipelining at all

q.q: What is a co-processor?
o: A second CPU that runs a copy of the operating system
An additional processor that takes a particular type of work off the CPU
A register that holds results while the CPU is busy
The part of the CPU that decodes each instruction
q.why: A GPU is the most important example of a co-processor.

It applies one instruction to over two million independent pixels at once
It runs the operating system while drawing the frame
It processes the pixels one after another very quickly
q.why: SIMD: single instruction, multiple data, across many simple cores.

q.q: Which is a limitation of using a GPU for general-purpose processing?
o: It cannot carry out floating-point arithmetic
It has too few cores for parallel work
Data must be copied to the GPU's own memory, which takes time
It cannot be used for machine learning

q.q: Which design is most suitable for a washing machine controller?
